0.title: The Word That Outlasts the Kings

1.text: <sup>1</sup>After the death of Ahab, Moab rebelled against Israel.<sup>2</sup>Now Ahaziah fell through the lattice in his upper chamber in Samaria, and lay sick; so he sent messengers, telling them, "Go, inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron, whether I shall recover from this sickness."<sup>3</sup>But the angel of the LORD said to Elijah the Tishbite, "Arise, go up to meet the messengers of the king of Samaria, and say to them, 'Is it because there is no God in Israel that you are going to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron?<sup>4</sup>Now therefore thus says the LORD, You shall not come down from the bed to which you have gone up, but you shall surely die.'" So Elijah went.<sup>5</sup>The messengers returned to the king, and he said to them, "Why have you returned?"<sup>6</sup>And they said to him, "There came a man to meet us, and said to us, 'Go back to the king who sent you, and say to him, Thus says the LORD, Is it because there is no God in Israel that you are sending to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron? Therefore you shall not come down from the bed to which you have gone up, but you shall surely die.'"<sup>7</sup>He said to them, "What kind of man was he who came to meet you and told you these things?"<sup>8</sup>They answered him, "He wore a garment of hair, with a belt of leather about his waist." And he said, "It is Elijah the Tishbite."<sup>9</sup>Then the king sent to him a captain of fifty men with his fifty. He went up to Elijah, who was sitting on the top of a hill, and said to him, "O man of God, the king says, 'Come down.'"<sup>10</sup>But Elijah answered the captain of fifty, "If I am a man of God, let fire come down from heaven and consume you and your fifty." Then fire came down from heaven and consumed him and his fifty.<sup>11</sup>Again the king sent to him another captain of fifty men with his fifty. And he answered and said to him, "O man of God, this is the king's order, 'Come down quickly!'"<sup>12</sup>But Elijah answered them, "If I am a man of God, let fire come down from heaven and consume you and your fifty." Then the fire of God came down from heaven and consumed him and his fifty.<sup>13</sup>Again the king sent the captain of a third fifty with his fifty. And the third captain of fifty went up and came and fell on his knees before Elijah and entreated him, "O man of God, please let my life, and the life of these fifty servants of yours, be precious in your sight.<sup>14</sup>Behold, fire came down from heaven and consumed the two former captains of fifty men with their fifties, but now let my life be precious in your sight."<sup>15</sup>Then the angel of the LORD said to Elijah, "Go down with him; do not be afraid of him." So he arose and went down with him to the king<sup>16</sup>and said to him, "Thus says the LORD, 'Because you have sent messengers to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron—is it because there is no God in Israel to inquire of his word?—therefore you shall not come down from the bed to which you have gone up, but you shall surely die.'"<sup>17</sup>So he died according to the word of the LORD that Elijah had spoken. Jehoram became king in his place in the second year of Jehoram the son of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, because Ahaziah had no son.<sup>18</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Ahaziah that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?
1.overview:
The book opens in the middle of a sentence. 1 Kings closed with Ahab's son serving Baal and provoking the LORD in every way his father had; here he goes through a window screen in an upper room, cannot get up, and sends forty miles to a Philistine shrine to ask whether he will recover.

Elijah is sent to meet the messengers on the road with a question that is asked three times before the chapter ends: is it because there is no God in Israel? (vv. 3, 6, 16). The king's answer is to send fifty soldiers to arrest the prophet, and then another fifty with the order made more urgent; and then a third captain climbs the hill, having watched a hundred and two men die, and goes down on his knees instead, and every one of his fifty walks home.

Elijah is told not to be afraid, goes down, and says the same thing to the king's face that he said on the road. So he died according to the word of the LORD that Elijah had spoken (v. 17). And in that verse a second Jehoram appears — one king of that name in each kingdom, at the same time, brothers-in-law through Athaliah — which the reader must sort out now or be lost for ten chapters.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Is There No God in Israel?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ahab's empire begins coming apart the week he dies — Moab rebelled against Israel (v. 1) — and his son goes through a window screen in an upper room and cannot get up. What he does next is the chapter: go, inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron, whether I shall recover from this sickness (v. 2). Elijah is sent to intercept the messengers on the road with a question and a sentence: is it because there is no God in Israel that you are going to inquire of Baal-zebub?... you shall surely die (vv. 3-4). The messengers come back far too soon, and the king asks what the man looked like. He wore a garment of hair, with a belt of leather about his waist — and Ahaziah names him from the clothes alone (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: The question is asked three times in eighteen verses (vv. 3, 6, 16), and it is not the question we would have asked. Not why are you consulting an idol, but is there no God in Israel — a question that assumes the thing the king has managed to forget. There is a God in Israel. He is the whole reason the country exists.
verseByVerse.examples: And the clothes are a uniform. Eight centuries later a man comes out of the Judean desert wearing a garment of camel's hair and a leather belt around his waist (Matt. 3:4), and of him the Lord says he is Elijah who is to come (Matt. 11:14). Malachi had promised it (Mal. 4:5). The costume was a signal, and the people who saw it read it.

verseByVerse.quote: After the death of Ahab, Moab rebelled against Israel. Now Ahaziah fell through the lattice in his upper chamber in Samaria, and lay sick; so he sent messengers, telling them, "Go, inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron, whether I shall recover from this sickness." But the angel of the LORD said to Elijah the Tishbite, "Arise, go up to meet the messengers of the king of Samaria, and say to them, 'Is it because there is no God in Israel that you are going to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron? Now therefore thus says the LORD, You shall not come down from the bed to which you have gone up, but you shall surely die.'" So Elijah went. The messengers returned to the king, and he said to them, "Why have you returned?" And they said to him, "There came a man to meet us, and said to us, 'Go back to the king who sent you, and say to him, Thus says the LORD, Is it because there is no God in Israel that you are sending to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron? Therefore you shall not come down from the bed to which you have gone up, but you shall surely die.'" He said to them, "What kind of man was he who came to meet you and told you these things?" They answered him, "He wore a garment of hair, with a belt of leather about his waist." And he said, "It is Elijah the Tishbite."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'After the death of Ahab, Moab rebelled against Israel.'

One sentence, and an empire has started to come apart.

Moab lay east of the Dead Sea and had been paying Israel an enormous annual tribute — a hundred thousand lambs and the wool of a hundred thousand rams, as chapter 3 will tell us. The moment Ahab is in the ground, they stop.

We happen to have the other side of it: Mesha king of Moab set up a stone recording that Omri had humbled Moab for many days and that he had triumphed over Omri's son. Two accounts of one rebellion, from opposite ends.

'Now Ahaziah fell through the lattice in his upper chamber in Samaria, and lay sick; so he sent messengers, telling them, "Go, inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron, whether I shall recover from this sickness."'

A lattice is a wooden screen set across an upper window, cut in a pattern to let air through and keep the sun and the neighbours out. He leaned on it and it gave way.

That is how the reign of Ahab's son effectively ends. Not in battle, not by assassination, not by plague. He put his weight against a piece of decorative joinery in the palace his father built, and it broke, and he was carried to a bed he never got out of.

Then the errand, and it is worse than the fall. He sends to Ekron.

Ekron is a Philistine city, forty miles away, in a country Israel had been fighting for three centuries. Baal-zebub means lord of the flies, and it is almost certainly not what the shrine at Ekron called itself. The name attested in the region is Baal-zebul, Baal the prince, lord of the exalted house. Somebody in Israel has changed one letter and turned the prince of the palace into the master of the dungheap, and the writer of Kings keeps the insult.

The name lasts. Eight hundred years later, when the Pharisees want the worst thing they can say about Jesus, they say he casts out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons (Matt. 12:24; Mark 3:22). A local Philistine deity with a defaced name ends up as a title for Satan.

And notice exactly what the king wants from him. Not victory, not rain, not a son. He wants a prognosis. He is frightened about his own body and he wants to know whether he will live, and he sends past every prophet in his own kingdom to ask a foreign shrine.

'But the angel of the LORD said to Elijah the Tishbite, "Arise, go up to meet the messengers of the king of Samaria, and say to them, 'Is it because there is no God in Israel that you are going to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron?'

There is the question, and it will be asked three times before the chapter is over (vv. 3, 6, 16).

It is not the question we would have framed. We would have asked why he was consulting an idol, or what he thought a Philistine god could do for him. God asks something else, and it is far more wounding: is it because there is no God in Israel?

The question assumes the very thing the king has managed to forget. There is a God in Israel. He is the reason the nation exists at all; he brought them out of Egypt and gave them the land and put this man's great-grandfather's dynasty on the throne, and there are prophets of his living in caves forty minutes from the palace. Ahaziah has not concluded that God is unavailable. He has simply not thought of him.

Take the question into your own week, because it travels without any adjustment at all. When the scan result is pending, when the letter arrives, when you cannot sleep for the thing you are frightened of — where does the first enquiry go? Not the second or the tenth, after prayer has been tried and found slow. The first. Most of us are not tempted to abandon God. We are tempted to consult him fourth.

'Now therefore thus says the LORD, You shall not come down from the bed to which you have gone up, but you shall surely die.'" So Elijah went.'

The sentence is put with a grim little play on words. You went up to that bed; you will not come down from it. And in ten verses the king will be sending men up a hill to order Elijah to come down.

'The messengers returned to the king, and he said to them, "Why have you returned?"'

They are back within the hour, and everyone in the room knows they cannot have been to Ekron. It is a forty-mile journey each way.

'And they said to him, "There came a man to meet us, and said to us, 'Go back to the king who sent you, and say to him, Thus says the LORD, Is it because there is no God in Israel that you are sending to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron? Therefore you shall not come down from the bed to which you have gone up, but you shall surely die.'"'

They repeat it word for word, including the question. Whoever he was, he made an impression, and they did not think of arguing.

'He said to them, "What kind of man was he who came to meet you and told you these things?"'

'They answered him, "He wore a garment of hair, with a belt of leather about his waist." And he said, "It is Elijah the Tishbite."'

They do not know his name. They describe his clothes, and the king identifies him instantly.

That is the measure of what Elijah has been to that family. Ahaziah has never met him, so far as we are told; his father hunted him through every kingdom in the region and called him my enemy, and the son can name him from a description of what he is wearing.

And keep the description, because it becomes a uniform. Eight centuries later a man comes out of the wilderness by the Jordan wearing a garment of camel's hair and a leather belt around his waist (Matt. 3:4; Mark 1:6), eating what the desert provides, telling a king to his face about his marriage. Malachi had closed the Old Testament by promising I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and awesome day of the LORD comes (Mal. 4:5), and Jesus said of John, if you are willing to accept it, he is Elijah who is to come (Matt. 11:14).

The clothes were a sign, and the crowds who went out to look at him could read it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–15 — If I Am a Man of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king's answer to a death sentence is to send soldiers. A captain with fifty men climbs the hill and gives an order — O man of God, the king says, come down (v. 9) — and Elijah replies with a condition rather than a curse: if I am a man of God, let fire come down from heaven and consume you and your fifty (v. 10). It does. A second captain comes with the same order and the word quickly added, and the same thing happens (vv. 11-12). The third comes up and goes down on his knees: please let my life, and the life of these fifty servants of yours, be precious in your sight (v. 13). And the angel of the LORD says to Elijah, go down with him; do not be afraid of him (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: These are not messengers. Fifty armed men are sent to fetch a prophet who has just delivered a word from God, and the captain uses the title man of God and then overrides it with the king's order in the same breath. What is being attempted on that hill is the arrest of the word of God, and Elijah's answer puts the office itself to the test: if I am what he called me, let heaven say so.
verseByVerse.examples: And the third captain is the reason the chapter is not simply terrible. Same errand, same fifty men, same hill — and he comes up on his knees and asks, and every one of them walks back down. The difference between the two hundred and fifty-one men who went up and the fifty-one who came home is entirely a matter of posture.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king sent to him a captain of fifty men with his fifty. He went up to Elijah, who was sitting on the top of a hill, and said to him, "O man of God, the king says, 'Come down.'" But Elijah answered the captain of fifty, "If I am a man of God, let fire come down from heaven and consume you and your fifty." Then fire came down from heaven and consumed him and his fifty. Again the king sent to him another captain of fifty men with his fifty. And he answered and said to him, "O man of God, this is the king's order, 'Come down quickly!'" But Elijah answered them, "If I am a man of God, let fire come down from heaven and consume you and your fifty." Then the fire of God came down from heaven and consumed him and his fifty. Again the king sent the captain of a third fifty with his fifty. And the third captain of fifty went up and came and fell on his knees before Elijah and entreated him, "O man of God, please let my life, and the life of these fifty servants of yours, be precious in your sight. Behold, fire came down from heaven and consumed the two former captains of fifty men with their fifties, but now let my life be precious in your sight." Then the angel of the LORD said to Elijah, "Go down with him; do not be afraid of him." So he arose and went down with him to the king
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then the king sent to him a captain of fifty men with his fifty. He went up to Elijah, who was sitting on the top of a hill, and said to him, "O man of God, the king says, 'Come down.'"'

He has been told by God that he is going to die, and his response is to send troops.

Do not read this as the dispatch of a messenger. Fifty armed men are sent up a hill to bring in a prophet who has just delivered a word from the LORD, and the captain's sentence is a small masterpiece of insolence: he uses the title — O man of God — and then in the same breath overrides it with the king says. He acknowledges the office and issues an order to it.

What is being attempted on that hillside is the arrest of the word of God, and the whole apparatus of the state is being used to do it, exactly as it was used to file Micaiah into a cell.

'But Elijah answered the captain of fifty, "If I am a man of God, let fire come down from heaven and consume you and your fifty." Then fire came down from heaven and consumed him and his fifty.'

Weigh the first word, because everything turns on it. If.

Elijah does not curse them and does not call fire down. He takes the title the captain has just used as a lever and puts it to the test in front of fifty witnesses: you have called me a man of God while treating me as a man under orders. Very well. If that is what I am, let heaven say so.

It is the same test as Carmel, moved. There the fire settled who God was; here it settles whose man this is, and the answer comes from the same sky.

'Again the king sent to him another captain of fifty men with his fifty. And he answered and said to him, "O man of God, this is the king's order, 'Come down quickly!'"'

The king has just lost fifty-one men and he sends fifty-one more, with the word quickly added.

That is the most damning verse in the chapter. He has the report. He knows what happened on the hill. And his correction to the policy is to make the order more peremptory.

'But Elijah answered them, "If I am a man of God, let fire come down from heaven and consume you and your fifty." Then the fire of God came down from heaven and consumed him and his fifty.'

'Again the king sent the captain of a third fifty with his fifty. And the third captain of fifty went up and came and fell on his knees before Elijah and entreated him, "O man of God, please let my life, and the life of these fifty servants of yours, be precious in your sight.'

'Behold, fire came down from heaven and consumed the two former captains of fifty men with their fifties, but now let my life be precious in your sight."'

Here is the third man, and he is the reason this passage is not simply an atrocity.

He has the same commission from the same king, the same fifty soldiers behind him, the same hill to climb, and he has watched a hundred and two of his colleagues die doing it. He goes up anyway — which takes considerable courage — and at the top he does not deliver the order at all. He kneels. He calls himself and his men your servants. And he asks.

Every one of them walks back down alive.

The chapter is not about a prophet with a temper. It distinguishes with great precision between men on an identical errand, and the entire difference is posture. Two came to summon the word of God and one came to ask it for his life.

And the New Testament settles what a Christian may do with this passage, in a scene that quotes it. Going through a Samaritan village that would not receive him, James and John said, "Lord, do you want us to tell fire to come down from heaven and consume them?" But he turned and rebuked them (Luke 9:54-55). Some old manuscripts even add the words as Elijah did, which is certainly what the disciples had in mind.

They were not misremembering their Bibles. They had the precedent exactly right, and they had missed the change of era entirely. The fire on that hill fell on soldiers sent to silence a prophet, under a covenant with a nation, before the Son of God came into the world; and the two disciples who wanted to reproduce it were standing next to the one man who could have done it and had come to do the opposite.

'Then the angel of the LORD said to Elijah, "Go down with him; do not be afraid of him." So he arose and went down with him to the king'

Read the middle clause and let it be as strange as it is. Do not be afraid of him.

God finds it necessary to tell the man who has twice called fire out of heaven that he need not fear a junior officer. Which means he did. Elijah is on a hilltop with two smoking patches below him and the third detachment on its knees in front of him, and he is frightened of going down.

The reader has seen this before — a man who faced four hundred and fifty prophets and then ran from a letter (1 Kgs. 19:3). Whatever spiritual authority is, it plainly does not come with steady nerves attached. God does not rebuke him for it. He simply tells him it is safe, and he goes.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–18 — According to the Word of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elijah walks into the sickroom and delivers the message a third time, in person and unsoftened: because you have sent messengers to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron — is it because there is no God in Israel to inquire of his word? — therefore you shall not come down from the bed to which you have gone up (v. 16). So he died according to the word of the LORD that Elijah had spoken (v. 17). He has no son; his brother takes the throne; and the chapter closes with the standing formula (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: The prophet who would not come down when fifty soldiers required it walks down freely when God says go, and says the same thing to the king's face that he said on the road. Nothing is added for the occasion and nothing is taken off.
verseByVerse.examples: And now hold two names apart or the next ten chapters will be a fog. Ahaziah's brother Jehoram takes the northern throne, and the southern throne is held by another Jehoram, son of Jehoshaphat — the man who married Ahab's daughter Athaliah. Two kings, one name, one generation, and they are brothers-in-law.

verseByVerse.quote: and said to him, "Thus says the LORD, 'Because you have sent messengers to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron—is it because there is no God in Israel to inquire of his word?—therefore you shall not come down from the bed to which you have gone up, but you shall surely die.'" So he died according to the word of the LORD that Elijah had spoken. Jehoram became king in his place in the second year of Jehoram the son of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, because Ahaziah had no son. Now the rest of the acts of Ahaziah that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?
verseByVerse.commentary:
'and said to him, "Thus says the LORD, 'Because you have sent messengers to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron—is it because there is no God in Israel to inquire of his word?—therefore you shall not come down from the bed to which you have gone up, but you shall surely die.'"'

The third time, and this time to the man's face, in his own sickroom, with the court listening.

Nothing has been softened. He is standing over a dying man who has twice tried to have him arrested, and he says exactly what he said on the road, question and all. There is no bedside adjustment, no diplomatic phrasing, and equally no gloating.

Note the small expansion the third telling carries: to inquire of his word. That is what was available. Not an oracle from a shrine, not a reading of the omens — the word of the LORD, which had been coming into that palace through prophets for two generations and had never once been wrong.

And there is a quiet mercy in the visit that is easy to miss. The man could have died without ever seeing him. God sends the prophet down the hill, into the room, to say it to his face, which means that Ahaziah dies having been told the truth to the last hour by a living man standing in front of him.

'So he died according to the word of the LORD that Elijah had spoken. Jehoram became king in his place in the second year of Jehoram the son of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, because Ahaziah had no son.'

According to the word of the LORD. The refrain of these two books, and here it closes a reign of two years that began by walking in the way of his father and his mother.

Now stop and get two names straight, because the writer has just put them in one sentence and a reader who does not sort them out now will be lost for ten chapters.

Ahaziah has no son, so the throne of Israel goes to his brother, another son of Ahab and Jezebel, named Jehoram. At the same moment the throne of Judah is held, or shortly will be, by a different Jehoram, the son of Jehoshaphat. Two kings, the same name, the same generation, the two kingdoms.

And they are family. Jehoshaphat's son married Ahab's daughter Athaliah in the marriage alliance formed at the beginning of 1 Kings 22, which makes the two Jehorams brothers-in-law. That is why they will campaign together, and why, when Jehu finally comes for the house of Ahab, the king of Judah will happen to be visiting and will be killed with them, and why Athaliah will then be in a position to destroy the royal family of David.

Every one of those consequences runs out of a single friendly alliance recorded in eight neutral words.

'Now the rest of the acts of Ahaziah that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?'

The file is closed on a man who reigned two years, and what we are left with is a question asked three times to a court that never answered it.

There was a God in Israel. He had a prophet on a hill four miles from the palace, and he had been speaking into that dynasty since before this king was born, and the king sent forty miles in the other direction to ask a defaced Philistine name whether he would get better.

1.theology:
The question, three times (vv. 3, 6, 16). Not why are you consulting an idol, but is there no God in Israel? — which assumes the thing the king has forgotten rather than the thing he has denied. Ahaziah has not concluded that God is unavailable; he has simply not thought of him. That is the ordinary form the sin takes, then and now: not abandonment but a change in the order of enquiry.

Baal-zebub, lord of the flies (v. 2). Almost certainly an Israelite defacing of Baal-zebul, Baal the prince, the name attested in the region. The insult outlives the shrine: when the Pharisees want the worst charge available against Jesus they say he casts out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons (Matt. 12:24).

The uniform (v. 8). A garment of hair and a leather belt, and the king names the man from the description alone. Malachi promised Elijah before the day of the LORD (Mal. 4:5); a man appeared at the Jordan wearing exactly that (Matt. 3:4); and Jesus said he is Elijah who is to come (Matt. 11:14). The clothes were a sign and the crowds could read it.

If I am a man of God (v. 10). Elijah does not curse and does not call fire. He takes the title the captain used as a lever and submits the office itself to test. Carmel settled who God is; this settles whose man this is. And what the captains were sent to do was arrest the word of God with fifty spears.

The third captain (v. 13). Identical orders, identical fifty men, identical hill — and he kneels and asks, and they all live. The chapter draws its line with great precision, and it is drawn at posture, not at rank or errand.

And Luke 9:54. James and John proposed to do this to a Samaritan village and were rebuked for it, with the precedent remembered correctly and the era missed completely. Fire fell on soldiers sent to silence a prophet, under a covenant with a nation, before the Son of God had come. The two men who wanted to repeat it were standing beside the only person who could, and who had come to do the opposite.
1.examples:
Then: A king lay in the bed he could not get out of and sent runners forty miles past every prophet in his own country to ask a Philistine shrine, whose god's name his own people had rewritten as lord of the flies, whether he was going to live.

Now: Two things. First, the question travels without adjustment. When the scan result is pending, or the letter comes, or you cannot sleep for what you are frightened of — where does the first enquiry go? Not the second, and not the tenth after prayer has been tried and found slow. Very few people are tempted to abandon God. A great many consult him fourth, and the Bible's word for that is not backsliding but is there no God in Israel? Second, the third captain, who is the most encouraging man on the hill. He was not braver than the other two and he was not on a better errand; he came the same distance under the same orders. He simply came up asking instead of ordering, and that was the whole of it.

But Elisha said, "As the LORD lives, and as you yourself live, I will not leave you." So they went down to Bethel.<sup>3</sup>And the sons of the prophets who were in Bethel came out to Elisha and said to him, "Do you know that today the LORD will take away your master from over you?" And he said, "Yes, I know it; keep quiet."<sup>4</sup>Elijah said to him, "Elisha, please stay here, for the LORD has sent me to Jericho." But he said, "As the LORD lives, and as you yourself live, I will not leave you." So they came to Jericho.<sup>5</sup>The sons of the prophets who were at Jericho drew near to Elisha and said to him, "Do you know that today the LORD will take away your master from over you?" 2.overview:
The writer gives the ending away in his first sentence so that nothing depends on suspense: the LORD was about to take Elijah up to heaven by a whirlwind. What is left to watch is how two men walk the last few miles — and the route is Israel's entry into the land run backwards. Gilgal, Bethel, Jericho, the Jordan; the nation came in across that river on dry ground, and Elijah goes out across it the same way.

Three times he offers his successor an honourable exit and three times Elisha answers with the same oath. He asks for a double portion — the firstborn's share, not twice the power — and is told the condition is sight. Then the escort comes between them and Elijah is gone, and the man who asked God under a broom tree to take away his life is taken away without it.

What follows is a new ministry beginning as it means to go on. The right question at the river (where is the LORD, the God of Elijah?), a search party he lets go because arguing would settle nothing, a poisoned spring at Jericho healed at the source in the town under Joshua's curse — and, at the gate of the calf-shrine at Bethel, a crowd jeering at what God did that morning.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — I Will Not Leave You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The writer gives the ending away in the first line — when the LORD was about to take Elijah up to heaven by a whirlwind (v. 1) — so that nothing hangs on suspense and everything hangs on how two men walk to it. Three times Elijah says please stay here and three times Elisha answers with the same oath: as the LORD lives, and as you yourself live, I will not leave you (vv. 2, 4, 6). Twice the resident prophets ask whether he knows what is coming, and twice he says yes, I know it; keep quiet. Fifty of them follow and stand at a distance, and Elijah rolls up his cloak and strikes the Jordan, and the two of them cross on dry ground (vv. 7-8).
verseByVerse.theology: Follow the route on a map and it is Israel's entry into the land run backwards. Gilgal, Bethel, Jericho, the Jordan — the nation crossed that river on dry ground, camped at Gilgal and took Jericho. Elijah walks out of the land the way it was walked into, and the water opens for him as it opened for Joshua and, before that, for Moses at the sea.
verseByVerse.examples: And keep quiet is the truest thing Elisha says all day. He knows; he has been told twice by well-meaning men who wanted to make sure he had heard; and he does not want to discuss it. Anyone who has walked the last week with someone they are about to lose knows exactly why.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the LORD was about to take Elijah up to heaven by a whirlwind, Elijah and Elisha were on their way from Gilgal. And Elijah said to Elisha, "Please stay here, for the LORD has sent me as far as Bethel." But Elisha said, "As the LORD lives, and as you yourself live, I will not leave you." So they went down to Bethel. And the sons of the prophets who were in Bethel came out to Elisha and said to him, "Do you know that today the LORD will take away your master from over you?" And he said, "Yes, I know it; keep quiet." Elijah said to him, "Elisha, please stay here, for the LORD has sent me to Jericho." But he said, "As the LORD lives, and as you yourself live, I will not leave you." So they came to Jericho. The sons of the prophets who were at Jericho drew near to Elisha and said to him, "Do you know that today the LORD will take away your master from over you?" And he answered, "Yes, I know it; keep quiet." Then Elijah said to him, "Please stay here, for the LORD has sent me to the Jordan." But he said, "As the LORD lives, and as you yourself live, I will not leave you." So the two of them went on. Fifty men of the sons of the prophets also went and stood at some distance from them, as they both were standing by the Jordan. Then Elijah took his cloak and rolled it up and struck the water, and the water was parted to the one side and to the other, till the two of them could go over on dry ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now when the LORD was about to take Elijah up to heaven by a whirlwind, Elijah and Elisha were on their way from Gilgal.'

The writer gives away the ending in his first sentence, which is a deliberate choice.

There is no suspense in this chapter and there was never meant to be any. We are told at the top what is going to happen, so that our whole attention is free for the thing the writer actually cares about, which is how two men walk the last few miles.

'And Elijah said to Elisha, "Please stay here, for the LORD has sent me as far as Bethel." But Elisha said, "As the LORD lives, and as you yourself live, I will not leave you." So they went down to Bethel.'

Now watch the route, and keep a map in your head, because the writer has chosen every stop.

Gilgal, then Bethel, then Jericho, then the Jordan. That is Israel's entry into the land, run backwards. The nation came out of the wilderness, crossed the Jordan on dry ground while the water stood in a heap, camped at Gilgal and set up twelve stones there, and took Jericho.

Elijah is leaving the land by the road the nation came in on, and in a few verses he will cross the river dry-shod, in the opposite direction, and his successor will come back across it the same way. Nothing about this is accidental.

Then the exchange that will happen three times. Please stay here — I will not leave you.

It is not that Elijah wants to be rid of him. It is a test, offered three times over, and the terms are gentle: you may stop here with honour, nobody will think less of you, this next part is mine. And three times the younger man refuses in identical words, with an oath: as the LORD lives, and as you yourself live.

The oath will be familiar to anyone who knows the book of Ruth — where you go I will go... may the LORD do so to me and more also if anything but death parts me from you (Ruth 1:16-17). It is the language of a person attaching their whole future to somebody else's and refusing to be released from it.

'And the sons of the prophets who were in Bethel came out to Elisha and said to him, "Do you know that today the LORD will take away your master from over you?" And he said, "Yes, I know it; keep quiet."'

The same test from the other side, and it is worse, because it is done kindly.

These are colleagues. They come out to meet him with a piece of information they are quite sure he needs, and they put it as a question so as to be tactful about it, and it is the single thing in the world he does not want said out loud.

Yes, I know it; keep quiet. Literally: be silent.

Anybody who has spent a last week with someone they are about to lose has been on both sides of that sentence. The knowledge is not the problem. Having it turned into conversation is the problem, and the kindest people in the room are usually the ones who cannot leave it alone.

'Elijah said to him, "Elisha, please stay here, for the LORD has sent me to Jericho." But he said, "As the LORD lives, and as you yourself live, I will not leave you." So they came to Jericho.'

'The sons of the prophets who were at Jericho drew near to Elisha and said to him, "Do you know that today the LORD will take away your master from over you?" And he answered, "Yes, I know it; keep quiet."'

'Then Elijah said to him, "Please stay here, for the LORD has sent me to the Jordan." But he said, "As the LORD lives, and as you yourself live, I will not leave you." So the two of them went on.'

Three offers, three refusals, two well-meant interruptions, and the same words every time. The repetition is the point: this is not one impulsive decision but a man declining the same honourable exit at every town on the road.

'Fifty men of the sons of the prophets also went and stood at some distance from them, as they both were standing by the Jordan.'

Fifty men who will not come closer and will not go home.

They have followed all the way to the river and then stopped, and they stand in a group at a respectful distance watching two figures at the water's edge. It is the exact position a great many people occupy in relation to God: near enough to see, far enough to keep their footing.

'Then Elijah took his cloak and rolled it up and struck the water, and the water was parted to the one side and to the other, till the two of them could go over on dry ground.'

He rolls up the cloak he threw over a young man ploughing in a field, and hits the river with it.

Moses stretched out his hand over the sea and the waters were divided (Ex. 14:21). Joshua's priests put their feet in the Jordan and it stood in a heap and the nation walked over on dry ground (Josh. 3:15-17). Now the water opens for a third time, for one man leaving and one man watching, and the writer uses the same phrase the old accounts used: on dry ground.

Elijah has been placed, quietly and unmistakably, in that line.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–14 — Where Is the LORD, the God of Elijah?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ask what I shall do for you, before I am taken from you, and the answer is please let there be a double portion of your spirit on me (v. 9) — which in the law is the firstborn's share of an estate (Deut. 21:17). The condition attached is sight: if you see me as I am being taken from you, it shall be so (v. 10). Then chariots of fire and horses of fire separated the two of them, and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven (v. 11), and Elisha cries my father, my father! The chariots of Israel and its horsemen! and tears his own clothes in two (v. 12). He picks up the fallen cloak, goes back to the bank, strikes the water and asks the only question that matters: where is the LORD, the God of Elijah? (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: He is not asking to be twice the prophet his master was. He is asking to be treated as the eldest son of the house — to inherit the office rather than to outdo the man. It is the same instinct as Solomon at Gibeon asking for an understanding mind, and it is granted for the same reason: it is a request for what the work needs rather than for what the man would enjoy.
verseByVerse.examples: And notice the question at the water. Not where is Elijah? The cloak in his hand is a piece of cloth and he knows it. What crossed that river the first time was not a garment and not a giant; it was the God of a man, and that God is still standing on the bank.

verseByVerse.quote: When they had crossed, Elijah said to Elisha, "Ask what I shall do for you, before I am taken from you." And Elisha said, "Please let there be a double portion of your spirit on me." And he said, "You have asked a hard thing; yet, if you see me as I am being taken from you, it shall be so for you, but if you do not see me, it shall not be so." And as they still went on and talked, behold, chariots of fire and horses of fire separated the two of them. And Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven. And Elisha saw it and he cried, "My father, my father! The chariots of Israel and its horsemen!" And he saw him no more. Then he took hold of his own clothes and tore them in two pieces. And he took up the cloak of Elijah that had fallen from him and went back and stood on the bank of the Jordan. Then he took the cloak of Elijah that had fallen from him and struck the water, saying, "Where is the LORD, the God of Elijah?" And when he had struck the water, the water was parted to the one side and to the other, and Elisha went over.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'When they had crossed, Elijah said to Elisha, "Ask what I shall do for you, before I am taken from you." And Elisha said, "Please let there be a double portion of your spirit on me."'

Understand what he is asking, because the phrase misleads almost everybody who meets it.

A double portion is not twice as much power. It is a legal term out of the law of inheritance: when a man divides his estate he must give a double portion of all that he has to the firstborn, whether he likes him best or not (Deut. 21:17). Two shares to the eldest son, one to each of the others.

So Elisha is not asking to be twice the prophet Elijah was. He is asking to be the heir. The sons of the prophets are a family and there are fifty of them standing across the river; he is asking for the eldest son's place in that house, and for the responsibility that goes with it. He will call Elijah my father three verses from now.

It is the right request, and this history has recorded one other man given a blank cheque by God and answering it as well. Solomon at Gibeon was offered anything and asked for an understanding mind to govern with (1 Kgs. 3:9). Both men asked for what the work required instead of what the man would enjoy, and both were told they had chosen well.

'And he said, "You have asked a hard thing; yet, if you see me as I am being taken from you, it shall be so for you, but if you do not see me, it shall not be so."'

A hard thing, because it is not Elijah's to give and he knows it. So he attaches a condition, and the condition is not obedience or effort or worthiness. It is sight.

Keep that, because it is where this book is going. Four chapters from now Elisha will be surrounded in a walled town by a Syrian army, with a terrified servant beside him, and he will pray O LORD, please open his eyes that he may see — and the young man will look at the same hills he had been staring at all morning and find them full of horses and chariots of fire (6:17).

The gift Elisha is granted here is the gift he spends his ministry asking for other people.

'And as they still went on and talked, behold, chariots of fire and horses of fire separated the two of them. And Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven.'

Read the verse slowly, because it does not say what it is usually reported to say.

As they still went on and talked. There is no farewell scene. They are in the middle of a conversation, walking, and it simply stops.

The chariot does not carry him off. It separated the two of them — it comes between them, and Elijah goes up by a whirlwind. The horses and chariots are not transport; they are the escort, and their business in the verse is to part two friends who were still talking.

Now put this beside a broom tree in the wilderness south of Beersheba, where this same man lay down and asked God to end his life because he was no better than his fathers (1 Kgs. 19:4). God refused that prayer. He fed him instead, and gave him a mountain and a whisper and a successor, and now he takes him away without letting him die at all.

Only Enoch had ever gone like that — Enoch walked with God, and he was not, for God took him (Gen. 5:24). Two men in the whole Old Testament, and one of them had asked to be allowed to die.

Nor is he finished. Nine hundred years later, on a mountain in Galilee, two men appear in glory and stand talking with Jesus about the exodus he is to accomplish at Jerusalem, and they are Moses and Elijah (Luke 9:30-31). Moses died, and God buried him in a valley and nobody knows where. Elijah never died at all. Both of them are there, which tells you that the difference between those two routes matters less than we suppose.

'And Elisha saw it and he cried, "My father, my father! The chariots of Israel and its horsemen!" And he saw him no more. Then he took hold of his own clothes and tore them in two pieces.'

He saw it. The condition is met in three words, and the writer records it before the cry, so that we know the inheritance is secure before we hear the grief.

Then the cry itself, and there are two things in it.

My father, my father — which is the double-portion request again, said as a son rather than as a petitioner. He is not watching a colleague leave.

The chariots of Israel and its horsemen — that is a military term, and it is extraordinary. Chariotry was a nation's strike force, the thing kings counted and boasted about and bankrupted themselves for; Ahab put two thousand of them in the field at Qarqar. Elisha looks at one man going up in a wind and says: there goes the army.

He means it exactly. The defence of that country was never its cavalry. It was this.

Keep the sentence, because it will be said again. Fifty years from now a king of Israel will stand weeping over Elisha's own deathbed and say precisely these words to him — my father, my father! The chariots of Israel and its horsemen! (13:14). The same line opens and closes the ministry.

Then he tears his clothes, and the detail is better than it looks. He takes his own garment in his hands and rips it in two, and in the next verse he picks up his master's. The last thing he owned as a farmer's son from Abel-meholah goes on the ground in two pieces, and he puts on the cloak.

'And he took up the cloak of Elijah that had fallen from him and went back and stood on the bank of the Jordan.'

'Then he took the cloak of Elijah that had fallen from him and struck the water, saying, "Where is the LORD, the God of Elijah?" And when he had struck the water, the water was parted to the one side and to the other, and Elisha went over.'

He is alone on the wrong side of a river with a dead man's coat in his hands, and fifty colleagues watching from the far bank to see what he is going to do.

And he asks the right question. Not where is Elijah? — which is what the fifty will be asking within the hour, and what they will spend three days searching for. Where is the LORD, the God of Elijah?

That is the whole doctrine of succession in one sentence, and every church that has ever buried a much-loved minister needs it. The cloak is cloth. It parted no water on its own and it never will. What opened the Jordan an hour ago was not a garment and not a giant of a man; it was the God whose servant that man was, and that God did not go up in the whirlwind.

The water parts, and he walks across, and the ministry has changed hands.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–25 — Salt in a New Bowl
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The guild at Jericho sees him coming and says the spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha (v. 15) — and then asks to send fifty men out to look for the body, and keeps asking until he is embarrassed into letting them, and they search three days for nothing (vv. 16-18). The men of Jericho tell him their water is bad and the land unfruitful; he asks for salt in a new bowl, throws it into the spring, and says thus says the LORD, I have healed this water (vv. 19-21). On the road up to Bethel a crowd of boys jeers go up, you baldhead, he curses them in the name of the LORD, and two bears maul forty-two of them (vv. 23-24). Then Carmel, and Samaria (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology: Jericho is the town under Joshua's five-hundred-year curse, where Hiel of Bethel laid the foundations at the cost of his eldest son and hung the gates at the cost of his youngest (Josh. 6:26; 1 Kgs. 16:34). That was the last thing the reader was told before Elijah walked in. And the first public act of Elijah's successor is to heal that town's water, at the spring rather than downstream, so that neither death nor miscarriage comes from it any more.
verseByVerse.examples: And the fifty searchers are worth a moment. They had been told; they had said it themselves twice; they had just watched the Jordan open in both directions. They still wanted to send out a party. Faith does not remove the instinct to go and check, and Elisha lets them spend three days finding out, which is sometimes the only way anybody believes anything.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the sons of the prophets who were at Jericho saw him opposite them, they said, "The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha." And they came to meet him and bowed to the ground before him. And they said to him, "Behold now, there are with your servants fifty strong men. Please let them go and seek your master. It may be that the Spirit of the LORD has caught him up and cast him upon some mountain or into some valley." And he said, "You shall not send." But when they urged him till he was ashamed, he said, "Send." They sent therefore fifty men. And for three days they sought him but did not find him. And they came back to him while he was staying at Jericho, and he said to them, "Did I not say to you, 'Do not go'?" Now the men of the city said to Elisha, "Behold, the situation of this city is pleasant, as my lord sees, but the water is bad, and the land is unfruitful." He said, "Bring me a new bowl, and put salt in it." So they brought it to him. Then he went to the spring of water and threw salt in it and said, "Thus says the LORD, I have healed this water; from now on neither death nor miscarriage shall come from it." So the water has been healed to this day, according to the word that Elisha spoke. He went up from there to Bethel, and while he was going up on the way, some small boys came out of the city and jeered at him, saying, "Go up, you baldhead! Go up, you baldhead!" And he turned around, and when he saw them, he cursed them in the name of the LORD. And two she-bears came out of the woods and tore forty-two of the boys. From there he went on to Mount Carmel, and from there he returned to Samaria.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now when the sons of the prophets who were at Jericho saw him opposite them, they said, "The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha." And they came to meet him and bowed to the ground before him.'

They watched the river open for him and drew the obvious conclusion, and they came out and bowed. The succession is recognised by the men who were standing at a distance, on the evidence of the one thing that could not be arranged.

'And they said to him, "Behold now, there are with your servants fifty strong men. Please let them go and seek your master. It may be that the Spirit of the LORD has caught him up and cast him upon some mountain or into some valley." And he said, "You shall not send."'

Then, in the very next breath, they ask to send out a search party.

Take stock of what these fifty men have. They had been told that day that the LORD was taking his master. They had said it themselves, out loud, twice, in two towns. They had just watched the Jordan divide in both directions. And their proposal is a mountain-and-valley search for a body, on the theory that the Spirit picked him up and put him down somewhere inconvenient.

'But when they urged him till he was ashamed, he said, "Send." They sent therefore fifty men. And for three days they sought him but did not find him.'

Till he was ashamed. They kept on at him until it was easier to give in than to keep refusing, and he let them go.

That is a very human piece of leadership and it is not held against him. He had told them the truth once, plainly. He did not need to win the argument, and he judged that three days of searching would settle it better than three hours of insisting.

Faith does not remove the instinct to go and check. Believing a thing and being able to stop looking for the body are two different accomplishments, and the gap between them is where most of us live.

'And they came back to him while he was staying at Jericho, and he said to them, "Did I not say to you, 'Do not go'?"'

He does not rub it in. One question, and the matter is closed, and the fifty now know something they would never have accepted on his authority alone.

'Now the men of the city said to Elisha, "Behold, the situation of this city is pleasant, as my lord sees, but the water is bad, and the land is unfruitful."'

Now stop, because of where this is happening.

This is Jericho. Joshua stood in front of its ruins five centuries ago and said cursed before the LORD be the man who rises up and rebuilds this city. At the cost of his firstborn shall he lay its foundation, and at the cost of his youngest son shall he set up its gates (Josh. 6:26). And in Ahab's reign a man from Bethel named Hiel rebuilt it anyway, and buried his eldest son when the foundations went in and his youngest when the gates went up — which is the very last thing the reader is told before Elijah walks into the throne room and shuts the sky (1 Kgs. 16:34).

Here are the men of that town, telling the new prophet that the site is lovely, the water kills, and nothing will grow.

'He said, "Bring me a new bowl, and put salt in it." So they brought it to him.'

'Then he went to the spring of water and threw salt in it and said, "Thus says the LORD, I have healed this water; from now on neither death nor miscarriage shall come from it."'

Two details carry the meaning.

He goes to the spring. Not to the pools in the town where the water is drunk, but up to the source it all comes out of. Whatever is wrong is dealt with where it starts, which is the only place anything is ever actually dealt with.

He also says I have healed this water in the name of the LORD. The salt is not a remedy — salt kills ground, it does not sweeten it, and a handful of it thrown into a spring is a sign and nothing more. The bowl is new because it has never been used for anything else. The whole procedure is designed to make it impossible to credit the technique.

Neither death nor miscarriage. That is what had been coming out of that spring: children lost before they were born, in the town where a builder had buried two sons under a curse. And the first public act of Elijah's heir is to go to that place and take it away.

Set the two scenes side by side, because the writer plainly means us to. In one, a man defies an old word of God and pays for it in his children. In the other, a man speaks a new word of God over the same water and the children live.

'So the water has been healed to this day, according to the word that Elisha spoke.'

Still good when the account was written, generations later. The spring at Jericho runs today.

'He went up from there to Bethel, and while he was going up on the way, some small boys came out of the city and jeered at him, saying, "Go up, you baldhead! Go up, you baldhead!"'

'And he turned around, and when he saw them, he cursed them in the name of the LORD. And two she-bears came out of the woods and tore forty-two of the boys.'

This passage is used to embarrass Christians more than almost any other in the Old Testament, and it should be dealt with properly rather than hurried past. Four things need saying, and none of them makes it comfortable.

First, who they are. The Hebrew word behind small boys covers a very wide range — it is used of Joseph at seventeen and of Solomon calling himself a child on the day he took the throne. Small pushes it younger, and the picture is certainly of youths rather than men; but the group is large enough that forty-two of them are caught, which is a crowd coming out of a town gate, not three children playing in a lane.

Second, and most important, what they are saying. Go up is not a general insult. That is the word this chapter has just used four times for what happened to Elijah — he went up by a whirlwind. A crowd from Bethel comes out onto the road and tells his successor to clear off after his master: go up, then, like he did. They are jeering at the thing God did that morning, and they are doing it to the man who was given the office.

Third, where. Bethel is not a neutral town. It is where Jeroboam put one of the two golden calves and built the rival sanctuary that every king of Israel since has maintained. The reception committee for the LORD's prophet at the gate of the calf-shrine tells him to go away and die.

Fourth, what Elisha actually does. He does not attack them and does not call for bears. He cursed them in the name of the LORD — that is, he pronounced a covenant curse, and the covenant itself names this exact penalty: I will let loose the wild beasts against you, which shall bereave you of your children (Lev. 26:21-22). He invokes a published sanction; God decides whether to enforce it. And the text says the bears tore them, which is mauling, not necessarily killing.

It stays severe, and Scripture makes no apology for it. What is being defended on that road is not a prophet's dignity or his hairline. It is the office, in the week it changed hands, at the gate of the town that had spent a century teaching Israel to worship a calf.

'From there he went on to Mount Carmel, and from there he returned to Samaria.'

Carmel is where his master had his greatest day, and he goes there first, and then down into Samaria, which is where his master's enemies live.

Elijah spent his life running towards that capital and away from it, hiding in ravines and foreign towns and caves in the far south. His successor walks into the city and stays, and for the next fifty years the prophet of the LORD will be a fixture there — advising kings, healing generals, feeding companies of the poor, and outliving four dynasties.

The cloak has been picked up, and it is being worn differently.

2.theology:
The double portion (v. 9). Not twice the power but the firstborn's share of an estate (Deut. 21:17). Elisha is asking for the heir's place in a family of prophets, and for the responsibility attached — the same instinct as Solomon asking for an understanding mind rather than for long life or riches. Both men asked for what the work required instead of what the man would enjoy.

The condition is sight (v. 10). Not obedience, effort or worthiness — whether he is given eyes to see what is actually there. That is what this book keeps returning to, and four chapters later Elisha prays it for a terrified servant: O LORD, please open his eyes that he may see, and the hills he had stared at all morning turn out to be full of horses and chariots of fire (6:17).

What the verse does and does not say (v. 11). The chariot does not carry Elijah off; it separated the two of them, and he goes up by the whirlwind. There is no farewell — they are still talking when it happens. And the man taken without dying is the man who had asked to die (1 Kgs. 19:4). God refused that prayer and gave him this instead. He is seen once more, on a mountain in Galilee, discussing with Jesus the exodus he was to accomplish at Jerusalem (Luke 9:30-31) — standing beside Moses, who did die and was buried by God himself.

The chariots of Israel (v. 12). Chariotry was a nation's strike force and the thing kings counted; Elisha watches one man go up in a wind and says there goes the army. He means it literally. The same sentence will be said over his own deathbed by a king of Israel fifty years later (13:14), and it bookends the ministry.

Where is the LORD, the God of Elijah? (v. 14). The right question, and the whole doctrine of succession in one line. He does not ask where Elijah is — the fifty will do that, and spend three days on it. The cloak is cloth. What opened the water an hour earlier was the God of the man, and that God did not go up in the whirlwind.

Jericho healed (vv. 19-22). The town under Joshua's curse (Josh. 6:26), where Hiel had buried two sons paying for it (1 Kgs. 16:34) — and the first public act of Elijah's heir is to heal its water at the spring, so that neither death nor miscarriage comes from it. Salt kills ground; it is a sign, in a new bowl, arranged so that no one can credit the technique.

The bears (vv. 23-24). Four things, none of which makes it comfortable. Go up is the chapter's own word for Elijah's ascension, so the jeer is aimed at what God did that morning. Bethel is the calf-shrine town. Elisha pronounces a covenant curse, and the covenant names this exact sanction (Lev. 26:21-22). And the text says the bears tore them, not that they killed them. What is being defended is the office in the week it changed hands, not a prophet's hairline.
2.examples:
Then: Fifty men followed the two of them all the way to the river and then stopped, and stood in a group at a careful distance watching — near enough to see everything, far enough to keep their footing — and within the hour were organising a search party for a body.

Now: Three things. First, keep quiet. Twice, kind colleagues came out with a piece of information Elisha already had and put it as a tactful question, and both times he asked them to stop talking. Anybody who has walked a last week with somebody knows both sides of that, and the lesson is for the visitor: the knowledge is rarely the problem, and the people who cannot leave it alone are usually the kindest ones in the room. Second, the search party. Believing a thing and being able to stop looking for the body are two different accomplishments, and the gap between them is where most of us live; note that Elisha did not win the argument, he let them spend three days finding out. Third, the question at the river. Every congregation that has buried a much-loved minister asks where is Elijah? and grieves at the gap he left. The cloak was only ever cloth. The question that opens water is the other one.
